# Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property.*** Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
***Limits Retroactive Taxes.*** Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively.
A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
#### Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 42 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40 on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters.
This is because the courts could find that Proposition 42 conflicts with Proposition 40.

Backed by major donors including Sergey Brin, it is structured so that whichever of the conflicting measures receives more votes prevails. PUBLISHED: October 29, 2026 at 12:25 PM PDT | UPDATED: October 30, 2026 at 4:46 AM PDT

California’s proposed billionaires tax is losing support days before Election Day, according to the second major independent poll released this week.
Thursday’s poll by the Institute of Governmental Studies at UC Berkeley found 42% of likely voters in favor of Proposition 40 and 50% opposed (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408), with 8% undecided. In a mid-September Berkeley IGS poll, 45% of likely voters favored Proposition 40, while 42% were opposed and 13% were undecided. It would need majority support to pass.
The measure would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires.
A pair of statewide measures aimed at blocking Proposition 40, Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, remained short of the needed majority support, with opposition mounting, the poll found.
Proposition 41 had support from 38% of likely voters while 47% were opposed and 16% were undecided, compared to IGS’ mid-September poll in which 37% were in favor, 33% opposed and 30% undecided. Proposition 42 support remained at 43% as it was in September, while opposition rose to 45% from 34% and undecided fell to 12% from 23% last month.
Both also require majorities to pass. If either passes and receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, it could prevent the wealth tax from taking effect if courts find the measures conflict.

“These results suggest that neither the advocates of the wealth tax nor those seeking to block future taxes have managed to persuade a majority of voters to their sides,” IGS Co-Director Eric Schickler said. “This may reflect an electorate unhappy with the wealth and power of billionaires but also not sold on a specific solution.”
The poll was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25, 2026, among 2,787 registered voters, of whom a weighted subset of 1,477 had either already voted or were considered likely to vote in the state’s Nov. 3 election. The margin of error was plus or minus 3 percentage points for the subset of surveyed likely voters.
It is the second poll this week to find support for the Proposition 40 billionaires tax fading. A Public Policy Institute of California poll Tuesday found that support for Proposition 40 had fallen to 46% from 52% in a September PPIC poll (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/california-billionaires-tax-prop-40-poll/), while opposition had risen to 52% from 46% last month. That poll also found support slipping and opposition mounting to Propositions 41 and 42, though it found Proposition 42 maintaining narrow majority support among likely voters.
Nearly $400 million has been spent collectively on the three measures, among the most closely watched contests on the state ballot.
Proposition 40 is sponsored by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West (https://yeson40.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24260871789&gbraid=0AAAABC2lkj1e3wEbPnCvZ-bOGGsaK_t-C&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox9nBHZ3OyEIQScw49n6D-MdfgBQwJMBaAh2pUa8NPlFM70x2-SIRhkaAj4cEALw_wcB), which says it would help offset federal Medicaid cuts. It would impose a one-time, 5% tax, payable over five years with interest, on an estimated more than 200 Californians and certain trusts with a net worth — the total value of all assets and property interests worldwide — of $1 billion or more who lived in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026. Supporters include the California Nurses Association, independent Vermont U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna, a Fremont Democrat.
Opponents (https://votenoon40.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=NoOn40&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24164855903&gbraid=0AAAABEizAVbUeWDtCbY6DbtURFUEQVEPx&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox_dANRzR4IFRvRvjuHz_CZLLCxIH87pCX5Z85gPQ8lzTiWKkED9jxEaAp18EALw_wcB) include Gov. Gavin Newsom, the California Teachers Association and both candidates for governor — Democratic former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra and Republican former Fox News host Steve Hilton. They’ve said such a one-time, California-only tax wouldn’t provide recurring new funding and would drive wealthy innovators and job creators, hefty contributors to the state’s income tax revenues, to other states.
Proposition 41 would prohibit new state taxes that exempt their revenues from California’s spending limit and require audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Proposition 42 would prohibit new state taxes on the ownership of personal property, such as financial assets, and limit certain retroactive taxes.
While likely voters were cooling on the billionaires tax, support remained steady for Proposition 3, which would make permanent higher income tax rates on high earners that voters initially approved in 2012, then extended in 2016 until 2030. The higher rates kick in at incomes of $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers, increasing the rate on income above those thresholds from 9.3% to 10.3%. The top rates, which increased to 12.3% from 9.3%, kick in at $743,000 for single filers and $1.5 million for joint filers.
The IGS poll found that support for Proposition 3 has held steady at 54% while opposition has edged up slightly to 37% from 34%, and 8% remain undecided.
Support for another statewide measure aimed at limiting local tax measures, Proposition 43, continues to trail opposition, the poll found. Proposition 43 would require two-thirds approval for local special taxes proposed through citizen initiatives, which currently can pass by a simple majority. Special taxes, which fund specific purposes, already require two-thirds approval when proposed by local governing bodies.
The IGS poll found that while support for Proposition 43 grew to 36%, opposition also grew to 46%. In September, 31% were in favor and 40% opposed.
While the poll focused on tax-related measures, it also asked about another closely watched initiative, Proposition 39, which would require voter identification. Support slipped to 37% while opposition grew to 57% with just 5% undecided. In September, 39% were in favor, 52% opposed and 9% undecided.
Proposition 4, which would repeal a state prohibition against public financing for election campaigns, had 41% support and 35% opposition in the latest poll.

Tax the Top, Fix Housing, Back Becerra: Cost of Living Drives California’s Vote, AIMSA Poll Finds
Published Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 | 7:48 a.m.
Updated Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 | 7:48 a.m.
SAN DIEGO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct 27, 2026--
California’s election is being decided at the kitchen table. Seven in ten likely voters name an economic issue as the state’s top problem — cost of living (38%), housing (19%), and the economy and jobs (12%) — and their ballot choices suggest they want the bill sent to the top, according to a new poll by AIMSA, distributed by Quadratín California.
This press release features multimedia. View the full release here:
https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261027904374/en/ (https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261027904374/en/)
The poll results will be presented this morning to San Diego business owners at a breakfast briefing at the University Club in downtown San Diego, hosted by Quadratin California in collaboration with the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce, where AIMSA Director Jesús Javier García Ruiz will walk through the findings.
The survey of 2,000 likely voters, conducted October 19–24, finds a consistent pattern on the ballot. Proposition 3, which extends taxes on high incomes, has 56% support; Proposition 37, loans for middle-income homebuyers, 59%; and Proposition 1, affordable housing bonds, 54%. At the same time, 50% back Proposition 42, which would ban state taxes on personal property. The pattern suggests voters favor measures whose cost falls on a narrow group of taxpayers or that expand access to housing, and resist taxes that could reach their own households.
“The message from California voters is clear: affordability and economic opportunity come first,” said Tayde Aburto, President of the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce (HISCEC). “Behind these numbers are families working to make ends meet and small business owners navigating rising costs.”
The most closely watched measure, Proposition 40, a one-time tax on billionaires, leads 50% to 44%, a margin the report places within the poll’s range of error. Its outcome is likely to resonate well beyond California.
Politically, the poll reveals a paradox: only 45% of voters say the state is headed in the right direction, yet Democrat Xavier Becerra leads Republican Steve Hilton 58% to 34%. President Donald Trump’s approval among the state’s likely voters is just 29%, compared with 50% for Governor Gavin Newsom, suggesting the race is being shaped as much by views of Washington as of Sacramento. The race appears largely settled: 24% have already voted and only 13% say they could change their minds.
For voters of Mexican origin, the affordability squeeze crosses the border. Seventy-one percent of Latino voters were born in the U.S., yet 29% send remittances to their country of origin and 34% chose to answer in Spanish: for nearly three in ten, one household budget supports two economies. Mexican-origin voters back Becerra 66% to 25%, while Latinos of other origins vote almost exactly like the state as a whole (58% to 32%). And while 52% of Latino voters approve of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, only 41% approve of the U.S.–Mexico relationship.
Leo Espinoza, President of Quadratín California, said the findings place the voices of Latino and Mexican-origin voters — a community with strong ties to Mexico — at the center of the conversation about the state’s future.
A second wave of the AIMSA survey, in the field since October 26, will show whether the billionaire tax and other close measures move in the final stretch. The full report, with results by region, age, sex and party, all 14 propositions, and the module on Latino and Mexican-origin voters, is available to journalists. Jesús Javier García Ruiz, Director of AIMSA, is available for interviews.
Methodology
AIMSA independently directed, conducted and financed the study; Quadratín California is the media partner and HISCEC supports outreach. The survey combines 1,200 SMS-to-web interviews linked to the voter file and 800 online panel interviews, in English and Spanish, across seven regions, with an oversample of 800 Latino voters. The 95% credibility interval is ±3 points statewide and ±4.5 among Latinos, larger for subgroups such as voters of Mexican origin. Results are not a forecast.
About HISCEC
Founded in 2008, the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce advances entrepreneurship, digital innovation, financial education and economic opportunity for small businesses.
About Quadratín California
Part of the Quadratín news network, Quadratín California provides Spanish-language coverage of issues affecting California and the binational community.
About AIMSA
AIMSA is a public opinion research organization responsible for survey design, fieldwork, weighting and analysis.

: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
“It’s below 50%, and it’s trending down. Both of those are ominous signs,” DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is “still very close. I’m not saying it’s definitely going down, but it’s moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves.”
He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.

If all three measures fail, that still would be a victory for the billionaires who spent aggressively to tank the wealth tax.
Another notable finding was voters’ support of Proposition 3, which would make permanent a higher income tax rate on the wealthy (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) that funds education. A majority of voters — 54% — support continuing the levy, while 37% oppose it, according to the poll. DiCamillo says the disparity in support of the proposed billionaire tax and the extension of the existing wealth tax has been consistent in IGS’s polls, and is likely because of the differing foundations of the levies.
“Proposition 3 is already in place, and if you read the fiscal impact, if this were to pass, it maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual funding,” he said, “It’s a big revenue generator, and I think that is something that’s already in place.”
“Voters kind of understand the progressive nature of California’s tax system, and they kind of support that, but they don’t support nearly as much the idea of some new kind of tax, the wealth tax, which is taxing assets rather than income,” he said. “So that’s the distinction.”
These ballot measures are among 14 that voters will decide (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits) on Nov. 3, as well as statewide, congressional, local and judicial elections.

Among the other controversial measures is Proposition 39, a measure pushed by Republicans that would require all voters in future elections to show government-issued identification every time they vote in person or provide a special PIN or the last four digits of their Social Security number when submitting mail-in ballots.
The measure also would require the California secretary of state and county election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens by “using government data,” which according to supporters could include information in the federal Social Security Administration database, jury summons information and other government records.
Nearly 6 in 10 likely voters oppose the effort, while more than a third support it, split largely along party lines. More than half of voters who are registered as “no party preference” or with a smaller political party oppose the proposal, which DiCamillo said was an indication of trouble for the proposition given the state’s Democratic majority electorate and the proximity of the election.
“It’s hard for Republicans to push something over the finish line by themselves,” he said.
Other prominent ballot measures:
Proposition 43, which would prohibit local governments (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-43-threshold-local-special-tax-voter-guide) from imposing certain new special taxes unless two-thirds of voters approve the proposal. Such proposals need a simple majority vote to be approved. While 46% of likely voters oppose the proposal, 36% support it, challenging numbers this close to election day, DiCamillo said. “It needs to get to 50,” he said. “We’ll see how you do that this late in the campaign.”
Proposition 4, which would repeal a prohibition of public financing of campaigns (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide), allowing state and local governments to support candidates if they abide by several rules. Likely voters are evenly split about the proposal, with 41% supporting it and opposing it, and 18% undecided. “It’s close, but it’s still below 50%. Most voters tend to vote no in the late going if they’re not convinced,” DiCamillo said, adding that he viewed the lack of support among voters who do not affiliate with a political party as a signal of potential failure.
The poll of 2,787 registered California voters was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25 and has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points in either direction.

California’s proposed billionaires tax is losing support days before Election Day, according to the second major independent poll released this week.
Thursday’s poll by the Institute of Governmental Studies at UC Berkeley found 42% of likely voters in favor of Proposition 40 and 50% opposed (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408), with 8% undecided. In a mid-September Berkeley IGS poll, 45% of likely voters favored Proposition 40, while 42% were opposed and 13% were undecided. It would need majority support to pass.
The measure would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires.
A pair of statewide measures aimed at blocking Proposition 40, Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, remained short of the needed majority support, with opposition mounting, the poll found.
Proposition 41 had support from 38% of likely voters while 47% were opposed and 16% were undecided, compared to IGS’ mid-September poll in which 37% were in favor, 33% opposed and 30% undecided. Proposition 42 support remained at 43% as it was in September, while opposition rose to 45% from 34% and undecided fell to 12% from 23% last month.
Both also require majorities to pass. If either passes and receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, it could prevent the wealth tax from taking effect if courts find the measures conflict.

“These results suggest that neither the advocates of the wealth tax nor those seeking to block future taxes have managed to persuade a majority of voters to their sides,” IGS Co-Director Eric Schickler said. “This may reflect an electorate unhappy with the wealth and power of billionaires but also not sold on a specific solution.”
The poll was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25, 2026, among 2,787 registered voters, of whom a weighted subset of 1,477 had either already voted or were considered likely to vote in the state’s Nov. 3 election. The margin of error was plus or minus 3 percentage points for the subset of surveyed likely voters.
It is the second poll this week to find support for the Proposition 40 billionaires tax fading. A Public Policy Institute of California poll Tuesday found that support for Proposition 40 had fallen to 46% from 52% in a September PPIC poll (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/california-billionaires-tax-prop-40-poll/), while opposition had risen to 52% from 46% last month. That poll also found support slipping and opposition mounting to Propositions 41 and 42, though it found Proposition 42 maintaining narrow majority support among likely voters.
Nearly $400 million has been spent collectively on the three measures, among the most closely watched contests on the state ballot.
Proposition 40 is sponsored by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West (https://yeson40.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24260871789&gbraid=0AAAABC2lkj1e3wEbPnCvZ-bOGGsaK_t-C&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox9nBHZ3OyEIQScw49n6D-MdfgBQwJMBaAh2pUa8NPlFM70x2-SIRhkaAj4cEALw_wcB), which says it would help offset federal Medicaid cuts. It would impose a one-time, 5% tax, payable over five years with interest, on an estimated more than 200 Californians and certain trusts with a net worth — the total value of all assets and property interests worldwide — of $1 billion or more who lived in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026. Supporters include the California Nurses Association, independent Vermont U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna, a Fremont Democrat.
Opponents (https://votenoon40.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=NoOn40&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24164855903&gbraid=0AAAABEizAVbUeWDtCbY6DbtURFUEQVEPx&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox_dANRzR4IFRvRvjuHz_CZLLCxIH87pCX5Z85gPQ8lzTiWKkED9jxEaAp18EALw_wcB) include Gov. California’s proposed billionaires tax is losing support days before Election Day, according to the second major independent poll released this week.
Thursday’s poll by the Institute of Governmental Studies at UC Berkeley found 42% of likely voters in favor of Proposition 40 and 50% opposed (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408), with 8% undecided. In a mid-September Berkeley IGS poll, 45% of likely voters favored Proposition 40, while 42% were opposed and 13% were undecided. It would need majority support to pass.
The measure would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires.
A pair of statewide measures aimed at blocking Proposition 40, Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, remained short of the needed majority support, with opposition mounting, the poll found.
Proposition 41 had support from 38% of likely voters while 47% were opposed and 16% were undecided, compared to IGS’ mid-September poll in which 37% were in favor, 33% opposed and 30% undecided. Proposition 42 support remained at 43% as it was in September, while opposition rose to 45% from 34% and undecided fell to 12% from 23% last month.
Both also require majorities to pass. If either passes and receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, it could prevent the wealth tax from taking effect if courts find the measures conflict.

Published Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 | 7:48 a.m.
Updated Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 | 7:48 a.m.
SAN DIEGO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct 27, 2026--
California’s election is being decided at the kitchen table. Seven in ten likely voters name an economic issue as the state’s top problem — cost of living (38%), housing (19%), and the economy and jobs (12%) — and their ballot choices suggest they want the bill sent to the top, according to a new poll by AIMSA, distributed by Quadratín California.

https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261027904374/en/ (https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261027904374/en/)
The poll results will be presented this morning to San Diego business owners at a breakfast briefing at the University Club in downtown San Diego, hosted by Quadratin California in collaboration with the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce, where AIMSA Director Jesús Javier García Ruiz will walk through the findings.
The survey of 2,000 likely voters, conducted October 19–24, finds a consistent pattern on the ballot. Proposition 3, which extends taxes on high incomes, has 56% support; Proposition 37, loans for middle-income homebuyers, 59%; and Proposition 1, affordable housing bonds, 54%. At the same time, 50% back Proposition 42, which would ban state taxes on personal property. The pattern suggests voters favor measures whose cost falls on a narrow group of taxpayers or that expand access to housing, and resist taxes that could reach their own households.
“The message from California voters is clear: affordability and economic opportunity come first,” said Tayde Aburto, President of the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce (HISCEC). “Behind these numbers are families working to make ends meet and small business owners navigating rising costs.”
The most closely watched measure, Proposition 40, a one-time tax on billionaires, leads 50% to 44%, a margin the report places within the poll’s range of error. Its outcome is likely to resonate well beyond California.
Politically, the poll reveals a paradox: only 45% of voters say the state is headed in the right direction, yet Democrat Xavier Becerra leads Republican Steve Hilton 58% to 34%. President Donald Trump’s approval among the state’s likely voters is just 29%, compared with 50% for Governor Gavin Newsom, suggesting the race is being shaped as much by views of Washington as of Sacramento. The race appears largely settled: 24% have already voted and only 13% say they could change their minds.
For voters of Mexican origin, the affordability squeeze crosses the border. Seventy-one percent of Latino voters were born in the U.S., yet 29% send remittances to their country of origin and 34% chose to answer in Spanish: for nearly three in ten, one household budget supports two economies. Mexican-origin voters back Becerra 66% to 25%, while Latinos of other origins vote almost exactly like the state as a whole (58% to 32%). And while 52% of Latino voters approve of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, only 41% approve of the U.S.–Mexico relationship.
Leo Espinoza, President of Quadratín California, said the findings place the voices of Latino and Mexican-origin voters — a community with strong ties to Mexico — at the center of the conversation about the state’s future.
A second wave of the AIMSA survey, in the field since October 26, will show whether the billionaire tax and other close measures move in the final stretch. The full report, with results by region, age, sex and party, all 14 propositions, and the module on Latino and Mexican-origin voters, is available to journalists. Jesús Javier García Ruiz, Director of AIMSA, is available for interviews.
Methodology
AIMSA independently directed, conducted and financed the study; Quadratín California is the media partner and HISCEC supports outreach. The survey combines 1,200 SMS-to-web interviews linked to the voter file and 800 online panel interviews, in English and Spanish, across seven regions, with an oversample of 800 Latino voters. The 95% credibility interval is ±3 points statewide and ±4.5 among Latinos, larger for subgroups such as voters of Mexican origin. Results are not a forecast.

Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
“It’s below 50%, and it’s trending down. Both of those are ominous signs,” DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is “still very close. I’m not saying it’s definitely going down, but it’s moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves.”
He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.

If all three measures fail, that still would be a victory for the billionaires who spent aggressively to tank the wealth tax.
Another notable finding was voters’ support of Proposition 3, which would make permanent a higher income tax rate on the wealthy (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) that funds education. A majority of voters — 54% — support continuing the levy, while 37% oppose it, according to the poll. DiCamillo says the disparity in support of the proposed billionaire tax and the extension of the existing wealth tax has been consistent in IGS’s polls, and is likely because of the differing foundations of the levies.
“Proposition 3 is already in place, and if you read the fiscal impact, if this were to pass, it maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual funding,” he said, “It’s a big revenue generator, and I think that is something that’s already in place.”
“Voters kind of understand the progressive nature of California’s tax system, and they kind of support that, but they don’t support nearly as much the idea of some new kind of tax, the wealth tax, which is taxing assets rather than income,” he said. “So that’s the distinction.”
These ballot measures are among 14 that voters will decide (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits) on Nov. 3, as well as statewide, congressional, local and judicial elections.

Among the other controversial measures is Proposition 39, a measure pushed by Republicans that would require all voters in future elections to show government-issued identification every time they vote in person or provide a special PIN or the last four digits of their Social Security number when submitting mail-in ballots.
The measure also would require the California secretary of state and county election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens by “using government data,” which according to supporters could include information in the federal Social Security Administration database, jury summons information and other government records.
Nearly 6 in 10 likely voters oppose the effort, while more than a third support it, split largely along party lines. More than half of voters who are registered as “no party preference” or with a smaller political party oppose the proposal, which DiCamillo said was an indication of trouble for the proposition given the state’s Democratic majority electorate and the proximity of the election.
“It’s hard for Republicans to push something over the finish line by themselves,” he said.
Other prominent ballot measures:
Proposition 43, which would prohibit local governments (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-43-threshold-local-special-tax-voter-guide) from imposing certain new special taxes unless two-thirds of voters approve the proposal. Such proposals need a simple majority vote to be approved. While 46% of likely voters oppose the proposal, 36% support it, challenging numbers this close to election day, DiCamillo said. “It needs to get to 50,” he said. “We’ll see how you do that this late in the campaign.”
Proposition 4, which would repeal a prohibition of public financing of campaigns (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide), allowing state and local governments to support candidates if they abide by several rules. Likely voters are evenly split about the proposal, with 41% supporting it and opposing it, and 18% undecided. “It’s close, but it’s still below 50%. Most voters tend to vote no in the late going if they’re not convinced,” DiCamillo said, adding that he viewed the lack of support among voters who do not affiliate with a political party as a signal of potential failure.
The poll of 2,787 registered California voters was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25 and has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points in either direction.

: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
“It’s below 50%, and it’s trending down. Both of those are ominous signs,” DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is “still very close. I’m not saying it’s definitely going down, but it’s moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves.”
He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.

If all three measures fail, that still would be a victory for the billionaires who spent aggressively to tank the wealth tax.
Another notable finding was voters’ support of Proposition 3, which would make permanent a higher income tax rate on the wealthy (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) that funds education. A majority of voters — 54% — support continuing the levy, while 37% oppose it, according to the poll. DiCamillo says the disparity in support of the proposed billionaire tax and the extension of the existing wealth tax has been consistent in IGS’s polls, and is likely because of the differing foundations of the levies.
“Proposition 3 is already in place, and if you read the fiscal impact, if this were to pass, it maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual funding,” he said, “It’s a big revenue generator, and I think that is something that’s already in place.”
“Voters kind of understand the progressive nature of California’s tax system, and they kind of support that, but they don’t support nearly as much the idea of some new kind of tax, the wealth tax, which is taxing assets rather than income,” he said. “So that’s the distinction.”
These ballot measures are among 14 that voters will decide (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits) on Nov. 3, as well as statewide, congressional, local and judicial elections.

In addition to high-stakes U.S. House races, California voters in November also will weigh in on a slew of ballot measures.
July 6, 2026
Among the other controversial measures is Proposition 39, a measure pushed by Republicans that would require all voters in future elections to show government-issued identification every time they vote in person or provide a special PIN or the last four digits of their Social Security number when submitting mail-in ballots.
The measure also would require the California secretary of state and county election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens by “using government data,” which according to supporters could include information in the federal Social Security Administration database, jury summons information and other government records.
Nearly 6 in 10 likely voters oppose the effort, while more than a third support it, split largely along party lines. More than half of voters who are registered as “no party preference” or with a smaller political party oppose the proposal, which DiCamillo said was an indication of trouble for the proposition given the state’s Democratic majority electorate and the proximity of the election.
“It’s hard for Republicans to push something over the finish line by themselves,” he said.
Other prominent ballot measures:
Proposition 43, which would prohibit local governments (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-43-threshold-local-special-tax-voter-guide) from imposing certain new special taxes unless two-thirds of voters approve the proposal. Such proposals need a simple majority vote to be approved. While 46% of likely voters oppose the proposal, 36% support it, challenging numbers this close to election day, DiCamillo said. “It needs to get to 50,” he said. “We’ll see how you do that this late in the campaign.”
Proposition 4, which would repeal a prohibition of public financing of campaigns (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide), allowing state and local governments to support candidates if they abide by several rules. Likely voters are evenly split about the proposal, with 41% supporting it and opposing it, and 18% undecided. “It’s close, but it’s still below 50%. Most voters tend to vote no in the late going if they’re not convinced,” DiCamillo said, adding that he viewed the lack of support among voters who do not affiliate with a political party as a signal of potential failure.
The poll of 2,787 registered California voters was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25 and has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points in either direction.

PUBLISHED: October 29, 2026 at 12:25 PM PDT | UPDATED: October 30, 2026 at 4:46 AM PDT

California’s proposed billionaires tax is losing support days before Election Day, according to the second major independent poll released this week.
Thursday’s poll by the Institute of Governmental Studies at UC Berkeley found 42% of likely voters in favor of Proposition 40 and 50% opposed (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408), with 8% undecided. In a mid-September Berkeley IGS poll, 45% of likely voters favored Proposition 40, while 42% were opposed and 13% were undecided. It would need majority support to pass.
The measure would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires.
A pair of statewide measures aimed at blocking Proposition 40, Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, remained short of the needed majority support, with opposition mounting, the poll found.
Proposition 41 had support from 38% of likely voters while 47% were opposed and 16% were undecided, compared to IGS’ mid-September poll in which 37% were in favor, 33% opposed and 30% undecided. Proposition 42 support remained at 43% as it was in September, while opposition rose to 45% from 34% and undecided fell to 12% from 23% last month.
Both also require majorities to pass. If either passes and receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, it could prevent the wealth tax from taking effect if courts find the measures conflict.

“These results suggest that neither the advocates of the wealth tax nor those seeking to block future taxes have managed to persuade a majority of voters to their sides,” IGS Co-Director Eric Schickler said. “This may reflect an electorate unhappy with the wealth and power of billionaires but also not sold on a specific solution.”
The poll was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25, 2026, among 2,787 registered voters, of whom a weighted subset of 1,477 had either already voted or were considered likely to vote in the state’s Nov. 3 election. The margin of error was plus or minus 3 percentage points for the subset of surveyed likely voters.
It is the second poll this week to find support for the Proposition 40 billionaires tax fading. A Public Policy Institute of California poll Tuesday found that support for Proposition 40 had fallen to 46% from 52% in a September PPIC poll (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/california-billionaires-tax-prop-40-poll/), while opposition had risen to 52% from 46% last month. That poll also found support slipping and opposition mounting to Propositions 41 and 42, though it found Proposition 42 maintaining narrow majority support among likely voters.
Nearly $400 million has been spent collectively on the three measures, among the most closely watched contests on the state ballot.
Proposition 40 is sponsored by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West (https://yeson40.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24260871789&gbraid=0AAAABC2lkj1e3wEbPnCvZ-bOGGsaK_t-C&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox9nBHZ3OyEIQScw49n6D-MdfgBQwJMBaAh2pUa8NPlFM70x2-SIRhkaAj4cEALw_wcB), which says it would help offset federal Medicaid cuts. It would impose a one-time, 5% tax, payable over five years with interest, on an estimated more than 200 Californians and certain trusts with a net worth — the total value of all assets and property interests worldwide — of $1 billion or more who lived in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026. Supporters include the California Nurses Association, independent Vermont U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna, a Fremont Democrat.
Opponents (https://votenoon40.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=NoOn40&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24164855903&gbraid=0AAAABEizAVbUeWDtCbY6DbtURFUEQVEPx&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox_dANRzR4IFRvRvjuHz_CZLLCxIH87pCX5Z85gPQ8lzTiWKkED9jxEaAp18EALw_wcB) include Gov. Gavin Newsom, the California Teachers Association and both candidates for governor — Democratic former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra and Republican former Fox News host Steve Hilton. They’ve said such a one-time, California-only tax wouldn’t provide recurring new funding and would drive wealthy innovators and job creators, hefty contributors to the state’s income tax revenues, to other states.
Proposition 41 would prohibit new state taxes that exempt their revenues from California’s spending limit and require audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Proposition 42 would prohibit new state taxes on the ownership of personal property, such as financial assets, and limit certain retroactive taxes.
While likely voters were cooling on the billionaires tax, support remained steady for Proposition 3, which would make permanent higher income tax rates on high earners that voters initially approved in 2012, then extended in 2016 until 2030. The higher rates kick in at incomes of $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers, increasing the rate on income above those thresholds from 9.3% to 10.3%. The top rates, which increased to 12.3% from 9.3%, kick in at $743,000 for single filers and $1.5 million for joint filers.
The IGS poll found that support for Proposition 3 has held steady at 54% while opposition has edged up slightly to 37% from 34%, and 8% remain undecided.
Support for another statewide measure aimed at limiting local tax measures, Proposition 43, continues to trail opposition, the poll found. Proposition 43 would require two-thirds approval for local special taxes proposed through citizen initiatives, which currently can pass by a simple majority. Special taxes, which fund specific purposes, already require two-thirds approval when proposed by local governing bodies.
The IGS poll found that while support for Proposition 43 grew to 36%, opposition also grew to 46%. In September, 31% were in favor and 40% opposed.
While the poll focused on tax-related measures, it also asked about another closely watched initiative, Proposition 39, which would require voter identification. Support slipped to 37% while opposition grew to 57% with just 5% undecided. In September, 39% were in favor, 52% opposed and 9% undecided.
Proposition 4, which would repeal a state prohibition against public financing for election campaigns, had 41% support and 35% opposition in the latest poll.

Tax the Top, Fix Housing, Back Becerra: Cost of Living Drives California’s Vote, AIMSA Poll Finds
Published Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 | 7:48 a.m.
Updated Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 | 7:48 a.m.
SAN DIEGO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct 27, 2026--
California’s election is being decided at the kitchen table. Seven in ten likely voters name an economic issue as the state’s top problem — cost of living (38%), housing (19%), and the economy and jobs (12%) — and their ballot choices suggest they want the bill sent to the top, according to a new poll by AIMSA, distributed by Quadratín California.
This press release features multimedia. View the full release here:
https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261027904374/en/ (https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261027904374/en/)
The poll results will be presented this morning to San Diego business owners at a breakfast briefing at the University Club in downtown San Diego, hosted by Quadratin California in collaboration with the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce, where AIMSA Director Jesús Javier García Ruiz will walk through the findings.
The survey of 2,000 likely voters, conducted October 19–24, finds a consistent pattern on the ballot. Proposition 3, which extends taxes on high incomes, has 56% support; Proposition 37, loans for middle-income homebuyers, 59%; and Proposition 1, affordable housing bonds, 54%. At the same time, 50% back Proposition 42, which would ban state taxes on personal property. The pattern suggests voters favor measures whose cost falls on a narrow group of taxpayers or that expand access to housing, and resist taxes that could reach their own households.
“The message from California voters is clear: affordability and economic opportunity come first,” said Tayde Aburto, President of the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce (HISCEC). “Behind these numbers are families working to make ends meet and small business owners navigating rising costs.”
The most closely watched measure, Proposition 40, a one-time tax on billionaires, leads 50% to 44%, a margin the report places within the poll’s range of error. Its outcome is likely to resonate well beyond California.
Politically, the poll reveals a paradox: only 45% of voters say the state is headed in the right direction, yet Democrat Xavier Becerra leads Republican Steve Hilton 58% to 34%. President Donald Trump’s approval among the state’s likely voters is just 29%, compared with 50% for Governor Gavin Newsom, suggesting the race is being shaped as much by views of Washington as of Sacramento. The race appears largely settled: 24% have already voted and only 13% say they could change their minds.
For voters of Mexican origin, the affordability squeeze crosses the border. Seventy-one percent of Latino voters were born in the U.S., yet 29% send remittances to their country of origin and 34% chose to answer in Spanish: for nearly three in ten, one household budget supports two economies. Mexican-origin voters back Becerra 66% to 25%, while Latinos of other origins vote almost exactly like the state as a whole (58% to 32%). And while 52% of Latino voters approve of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, only 41% approve of the U.S.–Mexico relationship.
Leo Espinoza, President of Quadratín California, said the findings place the voices of Latino and Mexican-origin voters — a community with strong ties to Mexico — at the center of the conversation about the state’s future.
A second wave of the AIMSA survey, in the field since October 26, will show whether the billionaire tax and other close measures move in the final stretch. The full report, with results by region, age, sex and party, all 14 propositions, and the module on Latino and Mexican-origin voters, is available to journalists. Jesús Javier García Ruiz, Director of AIMSA, is available for interviews.
Methodology
AIMSA independently directed, conducted and financed the study; Quadratín California is the media partner and HISCEC supports outreach. The survey combines 1,200 SMS-to-web interviews linked to the voter file and 800 online panel interviews, in English and Spanish, across seven regions, with an oversample of 800 Latino voters. The 95% credibility interval is ±3 points statewide and ±4.5 among Latinos, larger for subgroups such as voters of Mexican origin. Results are not a forecast.
About HISCEC
Founded in 2008, the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce advances entrepreneurship, digital innovation, financial education and economic opportunity for small businesses.
About Quadratín California
Part of the Quadratín news network, Quadratín California provides Spanish-language coverage of issues affecting California and the binational community.
About AIMSA
AIMSA is a public opinion research organization responsible for survey design, fieldwork, weighting and analysis.

Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
“It’s below 50%, and it’s trending down. Both of those are ominous signs,” DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is “still very close. I’m not saying it’s definitely going down, but it’s moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves.”
He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.

If all three measures fail, that still would be a victory for the billionaires who spent aggressively to tank the wealth tax.
Another notable finding was voters’ support of Proposition 3, which would make permanent a higher income tax rate on the wealthy (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) that funds education. A majority of voters — 54% — support continuing the levy, while 37% oppose it, according to the poll. DiCamillo says the disparity in support of the proposed billionaire tax and the extension of the existing wealth tax has been consistent in IGS’s polls, and is likely because of the differing foundations of the levies.
“Proposition 3 is already in place, and if you read the fiscal impact, if this were to pass, it maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual funding,” he said, “It’s a big revenue generator, and I think that is something that’s already in place.”
“Voters kind of understand the progressive nature of California’s tax system, and they kind of support that, but they don’t support nearly as much the idea of some new kind of tax, the wealth tax, which is taxing assets rather than income,” he said. “So that’s the distinction.”
These ballot measures are among 14 that voters will decide (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits) on Nov. 3, as well as statewide, congressional, local and judicial elections.

Among the other controversial measures is Proposition 39, a measure pushed by Republicans that would require all voters in future elections to show government-issued identification every time they vote in person or provide a special PIN or the last four digits of their Social Security number when submitting mail-in ballots.
The measure also would require the California secretary of state and county election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens by “using government data,” which according to supporters could include information in the federal Social Security Administration database, jury summons information and other government records.
Nearly 6 in 10 likely voters oppose the effort, while more than a third support it, split largely along party lines. More than half of voters who are registered as “no party preference” or with a smaller political party oppose the proposal, which DiCamillo said was an indication of trouble for the proposition given the state’s Democratic majority electorate and the proximity of the election.
“It’s hard for Republicans to push something over the finish line by themselves,” he said.
Other prominent ballot measures:
Proposition 43, which would prohibit local governments (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-43-threshold-local-special-tax-voter-guide) from imposing certain new special taxes unless two-thirds of voters approve the proposal. Such proposals need a simple majority vote to be approved. While 46% of likely voters oppose the proposal, 36% support it, challenging numbers this close to election day, DiCamillo said. “It needs to get to 50,” he said. “We’ll see how you do that this late in the campaign.”
Proposition 4, which would repeal a prohibition of public financing of campaigns (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide), allowing state and local governments to support candidates if they abide by several rules. Likely voters are evenly split about the proposal, with 41% supporting it and opposing it, and 18% undecided. “It’s close, but it’s still below 50%. Most voters tend to vote no in the late going if they’re not convinced,” DiCamillo said, adding that he viewed the lack of support among voters who do not affiliate with a political party as a signal of potential failure.
The poll of 2,787 registered California voters was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25 and has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points in either direction.

# California’s Billionaire Tax Slips From 52% Support to 42%
California’s Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on all billionaires in the state if more than 50% of voters fill in the box for “yes” by Tuesday.
It’s going to be a close one and may not pass, based on the latest polling.
Back in May, the Public Policy Institute of California found that 54% of California voters said they supported the wealth tax, with 45% saying they’d vote no.
The more recent polling has shown it to be even closer, with a Public Policy Institute of California poll taken Oct. 16-22 showing just 46% saying they would vote yes and 52% voting no.
An even more recent poll by a different organization, the University of California Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies, taken Oct. 19-25, shows just 42% saying they’ll vote yes and 50% pledging to vote no.
...
Opponents of Prop 40 have successfully gotten two of their own propositions on the ballot, Proposition 41 and 42, which are essentially poison pills that would negate Prop 40 if it does pass.
Prop 41 is also close, with a recent poll from the Public Policy Institute of California showing 49% for no and 48% for yes.
The same pollster has Prop 42 at 51% yes and 47% no.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

and Life Savings, a coalition of

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property’s value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
PROPOSAL
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
YES ON PROP. 42: PROTECT YOUR RETIREMENT AND LIFE SAVINGS FROM STATE TAXES
California is now the third most expensive state to retire in the nation. Every year, higher costs and taxes make it harder to save. An April 2026 survey found 73% of Californians know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
CALIFORNIA CONSTITUTION CURRENTLY ALLOWS DOUBLE TAXATION
Yet, California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts, even though residents already pay income tax on that money when they earn it. This means politicians can tax the same money twice: once when you earn it, and again when it is sitting in your retirement funds or savings accounts. That’s double taxation!
In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts.
Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California-we need protections against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS
Prop. 42 amends the state Constitution to protect Californians from this double taxation by special interests and politicians. Specifically, the measure:
• Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts; • Prohibits retroactive taxes; and • Prohibits all new taxes on retirement and savings this year and in the future.
PROP. 42 PROTECTS ALL FORMS OF RETIREMENT FUNDS AND SAVINGS FROM NEW TAXES
Roughly 80% of Californians report having some form of retirement fund or savings, including young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; and retirees who depend on their savings for financial security.
This measure protects all forms of personal property from new taxes, including 401ks, pensions, IRAs and personal savings.
“Prop. 42 protects Californians’ savings and retirement. Whether it’s a union member’s hard-earned pension or a small business owner’s IRA, new taxes on retirement shouldn’t stand between people and the security they’ve planned for.” -Chris Hannan, President, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California representing hundreds of thousands of union construction trades workers.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS UNFAIR RETROACTIVE TAXES
The state should not be able to pass new taxes that apply retroactively to money that taxpayers earned in the past. Prop. 42 requires any new taxes to apply only after voters have approved them.
“It’s a question of fairness and common sense. People plan their retirement for years-they deserve stable, predictable rules that don’t change after years of saving and planning. Prop. 42 provides that certainty.” -Sean Morgan, licensed financial advisor
Prop. 42 is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers, retirees, including groups like the California Professional Firefighters and Disabled American Veterans, Dept. of California.
Californians are already struggling with high costs of living and high taxes. Many work their entire lives to achieve some measure of retirement security. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings.
You earned and saved it. Now we need to protect it. Please join us in voting Yes on 42. YesonProp42.org
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Shelley Huff , Commander
AMVETS, Department of California
Jennifer Yoder , Board Member
California Senior Alliance
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
THIS IS ANOTHER BILLIONAIRE-FUNDED TRICK
Don’t be fooled-Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes.
It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 is a billionaire-funded scheme designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. They’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
WHO’S BEHIND THIS? SOME OF DONALD TRUMP’S DONORS
The billionaires behind this don’t care about protecting your retirement savings. They’re protecting themselves. They’ve been getting out of paying their own taxes for years through loopholes and tax breaks.
This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
PROP. 40 WOULD ONLY TAX BILLIONAIRES’ $2 TRILLION IN WEALTH
The billionaires behind Prop. 42 have spread lies about the California Billionaire Tax (Prop. 40), trying to trick voters into thinking that their retirement and savings are at risk.
Don’t buy the fear-mongering. The California Billionaires Tax ONLY applies to billionaires. It’s about making billionaires finally pay their fair share so we’re not stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs.
Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 42
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42. This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot for one reason-because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on personal property. It’s about preventing one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
PROP. 42 WAS FUNDED BY BILLIONAIRES WHO WANT YOU TO PAY MORE FOR HEALTHCARE
One of Prop. 42’s main funders is Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin, whose wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 42 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders called this arrogant move by Brin “unacceptable.”
Donald Trump took money out of working peoples’ pockets and gave it to billionaires like Brin through massive tax breaks. Now, the billionaires backing Prop. 42 want YOU to pay more for your healthcare.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42 IF YOU SUPPORT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
We have a chance to make billionaires pay their fair share to keep hospitals open and healthcare affordable for California’s working families. Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 42
WHO SUPPORTS PROP. 42
Prop. 42 is supported by hundreds of thousands of seniors, veterans, firefighters, blue-collar workers, public-safety officers and working families because it protects the retirement and savings of ALL Californians from new taxes. Who opposes 42? One organization that wants to tax retirement accounts.
WHY WE NEED PROP. 42
Sacramento politicians and special interests have repeatedly tried to pass taxes on retirement and personal savings accounts in recent years. They’ve relied on a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows government to tax our income when we earn it, and AGAIN when it is simply sitting in our savings and retirement accounts.
CALIFORNIA IS EXPENSIVE ENOUGH WITHOUT DOUBLE TAXATION
Prop. 42 prohibits this double taxation by PROHIBITING ALL NEW TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS ACCOUNTS and other personal property, whether proposed by legislation or ballot measure, including proposals on this year’s ballot and in the future.
It is a comprehensive constitutional protection against politicians or special interests trying to tax our retirement funds and savings accounts.
WHO BENEFITS FROM PROP. 42
Prop. 42 protects the retirement and savings for all Californians-young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; retirees and veterans who depend on their savings for financial security.
You saved it. You deserve to keep it.
Prop. 42 asks a simple question: should California politicians have the power to tax your personal property, including retirement and savings accounts?
If you think your retirement and savings should be protected from taxes, vote Yes on 42.
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Chris Hannan , President
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
Brian R. Marvel , President
Peace Officers Research Association of California

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) on billionaires’ assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.

Mark DiCamillo, the poll’s director, said previous surveys showed support for Proposition 40 has been fragile, and the most recent shows its prospects have dimmed as election day approaches.
The increase in opposition to Proposition 40 is “broad-based and spans virtually all major segments of the electorate,” DiCamillio said. The ballot measure was leading in a Berkeley poll conducted just six weeks ago, albeit by a slim margin, so its reversal of fortune is significant, he said.
Advertisement
The declining support comes after an onslaught of money spent opposing Proposition 40, including a torrent of television and social media ads airing everywhere from NFL games to “Everybody Loves Raymond” reruns. Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of billionaires who resided in California as of Jan. 1, with some exceptions. Democrats and their allies are splintered over the proposal. Some, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argue it will prompt the wealthy to flee California, further harming its volatile budget, which is dependent on the state’s richest residents. The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling it a modest tax necessary to help Californians struggling because of cuts imposed by Republicans to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.
While Republican voters overwhelmingly oppose Proposition 40, nearly two-thirds of Democrats support it and more than a quarter opposing it. There is also a generational divide, with 6 out of 10 voters 65 years old or older opposing the measure, while more than two-thirds of those under 30 supporting it, according to the poll.
The findings are similar to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday, which found 52% of likely voters would vote against Proposition 40, while 46% supported it.
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California’s richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
“It’s below 50%, and it’s trending down. Both of those are ominous signs,” DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is “still very close. I’m not saying it’s definitely going down, but it’s moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves.”
He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.
